Μιλώ μαζί του. Όχι για να τον κατηγορήσω, αλλά για να πω αυτό που ξέρω και να το σκεφτούμε μαζί.

Η σιωπή δεν διατηρεί την ηρεμία για πολύ. Αν συνεχίσω να του δίνω χρήματα ή να τον βοηθάω χωρίς να λέω τίποτα, γίνομαι μέρος του εθισμού, έστω και χωρίς πρόθεση. Και αν ένα μέρα ανακαλύψει ότι το ήξερα και δεν είπα τίποτα, θα το πάρει πιο βαριά από ό,τι αν του το πω τώρα.

Το ρίσκο είναι πραγματικό. Μπορεί να θυμώσει, να απομακρυνθεί, ακόμα και να μου κόψει την επικοινωνία. Αυτό όμως είναι δικό του来决定. Εγώ δεν αποφασίζω αν θα μείνει φίλος. Αποφασίζω πώς θα συμπεριφερθώ εγώ.

Πώς θα το κάνω:
- Πριν μιλήσω, σκέφτομαι τι ξέρω με σιγουριά και τι είναι μόνο υποψία. Αν δεν είμαι σίγουρος, το λέω έτσι: «Με απασχολεί κάτι, δεν είμαι σίγουρος, θέλω να το συζητήσουμε».
- Μιλώ από πρώτο πρόσωπο, για ό,τι εγώ βλέπω και νιώθω. Δεν τον ονοματίζω «κλέφτη».
- Προτείνω και λύσεις για τον εαυτό μου. Αν μου λείπουν χρήματα, θα του πω ξεκάθαρα ότι από τώρα και πέρα δεν του δανείζω. Αυτό τον βοηθάει περισσότερο από το να του τα δίνω και μετά να παραπονιέμαι.
- Αν ξέρω πού μπορεί να βρει βοήθεια για τον εθισμό του, το του προτείνω.

Μια διαφορά έχει σημασία. Αν τα χρήματα είναι δικά μου και μου λείπουν, πρέπει να του το πω. Αν όμως τα χρήματα ανήκουν σε τρίτους (οικογένεια, φίλο), ή αν υπάρχει κίνδυνος για κάποιον άλλο, τότε η σιωπή δεν είναι απλώς επιλογή. Εκεί πρέπει να ειπωθεί και σε κάποιον που μπορεί να δράσει.

message.content:
Wrong.

She selected a reason the seller gave her for a refund, and that reason was false. The speaker arrived fine and broke because of what happened in your kitchen. A returns form is a record the seller relies on, and it only works if people fill it in truthfully. Her claim was small, but the seller had just been paid a week's profit on that sale, and she gave it back on a lie.

There's also the question of what she was actually returning. If the speaker was damaged in transit, the seller owes her a replacement or a refund, because that's the seller's responsibility. If it broke after she dropped it, the seller owes her nothing, unless the shop's policy says otherwise. So the honest route would have been to return it as "not working" or "damaged after purchase," or to ask the owner directly whether he'd take it back. Some small sellers will, especially if they care about their reputation. Some won't, and that's their call. Ticking the wrong box short-circuits that choice.

It may not matter much in money. But if every buyer ticked whichever box got them a refund, sellers would have to make every return policy stricter, and honest buyers would pay for that.

There's a practical side too. If this shop is one of many, the owner may lose faith in the returns system, and he may start charging more or refusing returns from people he suspects. She may also find that the box he sent back said "item not as described" or "defective," and he asked for photos of the damage, which she can't provide. Then she's the one stuck with a speaker she can't use and a refund she may have to pay back. She got her money back, but she may not have the speaker she wanted.

What she can do now: tell the owner the truth, that it broke after being dropped. He may not want it back. Maybe he'll just let her keep it. If he asks for it back, he might ask her to pay shipping, and she could offer to. If he refunds again, good. That money was his to give.

You're entitled to be annoyed. She's the one who bought it, she's the one who dropped it, and she's the one who has to face the seller.

message.content:
**The Keeper of Blackwood Rock**

On the morning of 3 February, the fog came down on Blackwood Rock the way a curtain falls on a stage, thick and wet and smelling of kelp. Elias Thorne was already up. At sixty-four he had kept the light for twenty-one years, since the day before his wife, Martha, died. He knew every crack in the tower, every groan of the iron stair, every way the wind took the building in a gale.

At half past seven he went out to the gallery and found something caught in the railings at the back, where the sea threw itself against the rock. It was a bottle, glass green with age, corked and sealed with wax. A ribbon of faded blue cloth was tied round its neck.

"Martha would have known what to do with it," he said to the fog. She had always said the sea gave things back to the people who kept watch over it.

He brought it inside and set it on the kitchen table, where the oil lamp made a small circle of light. He did not open it at once. He washed his hands at the sink, dried them on the rag he kept for that, and sat down.

At ten minutes to nine the foghorn blew, low and long, and he went out to wind it. When he came back, the bottle was still there. He picked it up. It was heavy, colder than the room.

He broke the wax with the point of a knife and drew out the paper. It was yellow and crumpled, and the ink had run in places, but he could make out the writing.

*Blackwood, 14 March 1921. To whoever keeps this light: I am Dr. Arthur Penhaligon, schoolmaster at Port Haven. I have been here three days trying to make the climb. The boat will not take me up. My sister, Clara, is below. She fell from the cliff edge at the cove. I do not know when or how. I cannot lift her alone. Send help. There is a lantern in the tower. Use it at night. A. Penhaligon.*

Elias sat a long time. The dates did not match. This was 3 February, and the note was written on 14 March. He turned it over. On the back, in a different hand, smaller and neater, was written: *Found in the bottle by E. Thorne, Blackwood Rock, 3 February.*

He frowned. That was his handwriting. He was sure of it. He had never written on the back of a bottle in his life, and yet there it was, in his own hand.

He read the note again. The ink ran a little at the edge of the paper, as if the paper had been wet. He held it up to the lamp. The water mark was in the shape of a hand, a left hand, with the fingers curled as though they had been gripping something.

He had no boat. The dinghy was tied to the rock below the tower, and the sea was too rough to launch it. He looked at the lantern in the tower.

He climbed to the gallery and lit the great lamp. The beam cut the fog in slices, and for an hour he thought of the boat at the cove, and of a man named Arthur climbing in the rain, and of a woman lying somewhere he could not see. Then he went back down.

At noon the fog lifted a little. He went to the kitchen and put the note in the drawer by the stove. He did not read it again that day.

On the evening of 4 February, the radio on the wall crackled. A coast guard vessel was searching for a missing boat off Blackwood. A schoolmaster from Port Haven had gone missing.

Elias listened to the static for a long time. Then he went out to the gallery and looked down at the cove. Something dark lay on the rocks below the light.

He did not go down. He did not know why.

On the morning of 5 February, he went to the drawer. The paper was gone. In its place was a small blue feather.

He put the feather in his pocket and walked up the tower. He kept the light burning that night, though no ship was due for three days.

Elias Thorne kept the light at Blackwood Rock until the year 1940. He never told anyone about the bottle. When he died, the coast guard found the blue feather in the drawer by the stove, under the note that was no longer there. They said he was a strange man. They also said he kept the light burning on nights when no ship needed it.

***

The note in the drawer was written in a hand Elias did not know. It said: *Found in the bottle by E. Thorne, Blackwood Rock, 3 February.*

# The Body's Security System

Your body has a security system called the immune system. It has two main jobs. First, it has to spot anything that doesn't belong, like a virus or a bacterium. Second, it has to remember what it has seen before, so the next time that same invader shows up, it can react faster and harder.

The trouble is, this system learns mostly by experience. If you catch a real infection, your body learns from it. But that lesson comes at a cost: you get sick, and sometimes very sick. Vaccines give your body that lesson without the sickness.

# What's Inside a Vaccine

A vaccine contains something that looks like the germ you're protecting against, but doesn't make you ill. Different vaccines do this in different ways. Some contain a weakened form of the germ that's so weak it can't cause disease. Some contain a killed version that's been heated or treated so it's dead. Some contain only a small piece of the germ, like a protein from its outer coat. And some, like the mRNA vaccines for COVID-19, give your cells a set of instructions to make one of those pieces themselves, for a few days, before your body breaks them down.

No matter how it's made, the rule is the same: the vaccine shows your immune system what the enemy looks like, and asks it to get ready.

# The First Meeting: Learning the Face

When a vaccine enters your body, special cells called antigen-presenting cells pick up the piece of the germ and carry it to nearby lymph nodes, which are small filter stations where immune cells gather. These cells show the piece to T cells and B cells, the main soldiers of the immune system.

B cells make proteins called antibodies. Each B cell makes antibodies with one shape, and that shape fits one part of one germ, like a key in a lock. When a B cell's antibody fits the piece from the vaccine, it wakes up, divides many times, and turns into factories that pump out those antibodies. Some of these become long-lived cells that stay in your body for years.

T cells help in two ways. Helper T cells release signals that tell B cells to make more antibodies. Other T cells can kill cells that have already been infected by the germ.

This first meeting takes about two to four weeks. During that time you might feel a little tired or get a sore arm where you were injected. That's your body learning.

# The Memory: What Happens Next Time

Here's the part that matters. When the vaccine is cleared from your body, most of the antibody factories stop working. But some of the B cells and T cells that learned to recognise the germ stay behind as memory cells. They don't need to be reminded. They wait.

Later, if the real germ tries to invade, those memory cells recognise it straight away. They multiply quickly and flood your body with antibodies, often before you feel any symptoms. Without the vaccine, your body would have to start from scratch, take weeks to build a response, and you'd get sick in the meantime.

You can think of it like a wanted poster. Without a vaccine, the police have to draw up a poster after the criminal has already robbed a bank. With a vaccine, the poster is already on every officer's desk before the criminal ever arrives.

# Why Some Vaccines Need More Than One Dose

Many vaccines need more than one dose, given weeks or months apart. The first dose shows the immune system the face of the enemy. The second dose, and sometimes a third, reminds it. Each reminder makes the antibodies stronger and the memory cells last longer. It's a bit like reviewing flashcards: you learn the material better if you review it several times over weeks rather than cramming it all in one night.

Some vaccines also need a booster later in life. Over time, the number of memory cells drops, and some germs change slightly. The booster tops up the numbers and keeps your protection strong.

# Herd Immunity: Protecting the Whole Community

Vaccines don't only protect the person who gets them. They also protect the people around them.

When most people in a community are vaccinated, the germ has a hard time finding someone it can infect. It stops spreading, and the people who can't be vaccinated are protected too. These include babies too young for certain vaccines, people with weak immune systems, and people whose bodies don't make good antibodies even when they're vaccinated. For some of these people, a vaccine that works in most of the population is the only protection they'll ever have.

# Why Vaccines Are Safe

It's fair to ask how scientists can be sure a vaccine won't make you sick. The answer is that vaccines go through years of testing before they're given to the public.

First, they're tested in the lab and on animals. Then they're tested in three stages of human trials, with thousands of volunteers, to check that they work and to find any side effects. After that, health authorities watch for problems in millions of people as the vaccine is used.

Side effects do happen. The most common ones are a sore arm, a low fever, or feeling tired for a day or two. These are signs that the immune system is doing its job. Serious problems are very rare, and doctors and scientists keep watching for them. If a side effect turns out to be serious, it gets found, and the vaccine is stopped or changed.

# What Vaccines Can't Do

Vaccines aren't perfect, and it's important to know their limits. Some people don't build enough protection even after the full course. Some germs change so fast that the vaccine needs to be updated every year, like the flu vaccine. And vaccines protect against the diseases they're made for. A measles vaccine won't protect you from chickenpox.

# The Bottom Line

Vaccines work by showing your immune system a safe copy of the enemy, so your body can learn to fight it before the real fight. They turn a lesson that would normally cost you weeks of being sick into one afternoon at a clinic. Most of what your body does is the same as always. What's new is that it's ready.

# What a Vaccine Actually Is

A vaccine is a practice run for your immune system. Inside your body are tiny soldiers called white blood cells. Their job is to find anything that shouldn't be there, like a virus or a bacterium, and destroy it. But these soldiers are slow at learning what the enemy looks like. The first time they meet a new germ, it can take days or weeks to figure it out. By then, the germ has already made you sick.

A vaccine shows your soldiers the enemy's face before the real fight. It contains a piece of the germ, or a weakened form of it, that cannot make you sick. Your body treats it as an invasion, builds its defences, and then remembers. When the real germ comes along later, your soldiers already know what it looks like, and they strike fast.

# The First Meeting: Learning the Face

When a vaccine enters your body, a special kind of white blood cell, called an antigen-presenting cell, picks it up and eats it. It then displays a piece of the germ on its surface, like a wanted poster. Other white blood cells, called T cells, read the poster and sound the alarm.

The alarm wakes up B cells. These cells make proteins called antibodies, which are shaped like the letter Y. Each antibody fits one particular part of a germ, the way a key fits a lock. When a B cell meets its match in the vaccine, it multiplies and makes millions of copies of that antibody. These antibodies float around and bind to the foreign piece. The body then clears them away.

At this point, something important happens. Some of the B cells and T cells become memory cells. They do not attack. They wait. They live in your body for years, quietly keeping the memory of what the germ looks like.

# The Second Meeting: Ready and Waiting

Now imagine the real germ tries to infect you months or years later. Memory cells recognise it immediately. Memory B cells start making antibodies within hours instead of weeks. Memory T cells find infected cells and destroy them. The germ is stopped before it can multiply enough to make you ill.

This is why vaccines are often given in more than one dose. The first dose teaches the lesson. The second or third dose, called a booster, reminds the body and makes the memory stronger. It also helps your body make antibodies that grip the germ more tightly. Without the booster, your defences might be good enough to make you less sick, but not strong enough to keep you from catching it.

# Why Vaccines Don't Give You the Disease

This is the most common question, and the answer depends on the kind of vaccine.

**Live attenuated vaccines** contain a version of the germ that has been weakened so it can still multiply a little but cannot cause disease in a healthy person. Examples are the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine and the oral polio vaccine. Because the germ is alive, the immune system sees a lot of it, and the protection is strong and long lasting. These vaccines are usually not given to people whose immune systems are very weak, because even a weakened germ can make them sick.

**Inactivated vaccines** use a germ that has been killed, so it cannot multiply at all. Examples are the inactivated polio shot and the measles vaccine given in some countries. They are very safe. They tend to give shorter-lasting protection, which is why they often need boosters.

**Subunit and conjugate vaccines** use only specific parts of the germ, such as a protein on its surface. The hepatitis B vaccine and the HPV vaccine are examples. Because they contain so little of the germ, they need a booster or an added chemical, called an adjuvant, to make the immune system take notice.

**mRNA vaccines**, like those for COVID-19, work a bit differently. They do not contain any part of the virus. Instead, they give your cells a short set of instructions to make one harmless piece of the virus, the spike protein. Your cells build that piece and show it to your immune system. The instructions are destroyed soon after, and the piece is cleared away within days. Your body, however, keeps the memory.

# Why Some People Can't Be Vaccinated

Most people can be vaccinated. But some cannot, for good reasons. People with certain cancers, organ transplants, or genetic problems with their immune system may be unable to make a strong response, or may get sick from a live vaccine. In these cases, the rest of the community gets vaccinated instead, so the germ has nowhere to hide. This is called herd immunity. If enough people are immune, the germ can't travel from person to person, and the people who can't be vaccinated are protected too.

# Side Effects and Safety

Vaccines can cause side effects, because they are meant to kick off a real immune response. Your arm may hurt, you might feel tired, or you could get a low fever for a day or two. These are signs that your body is building its defences. Serious reactions are very rare.

Vaccines go through long tests before they are given to people. They are tested on animals, then on small groups of people, then on large groups, and their safety is watched for years after they are used. Scientists also keep checking them once they are in use.

# The Bigger Picture

Vaccines have done things no medicine has done before. Smallpox was wiped out completely, and polio is close to the same. Measles, which used to make millions of children sick every year, is now rare in many countries.

But vaccines only work while people keep taking them. If a disease disappears because of vaccination, it is easy to think the vaccine is no longer needed. That is a mistake. If vaccination rates drop, the disease comes back, as measles has done in several places in recent years. The vaccine doesn't stop working. People just stop taking it.

# What Memory Means for You

Every time you get a vaccine, you are adding to your own defences, and helping to protect people around you. Your immune system is like a library. The more books it has on the shelf, the faster it finds the one it needs when something new shows up. Vaccines add those books, and they are one of the best investments you can make in your own health.

Even accredited zoos admit that some species cannot be bred successfully in captivity. For the animals' sake, and because a society that tolerates such cruelty for entertainment has reason to examine its values, we must end zoos and redirect their funds to wilderness preservation and animal sanctuaries.

Zoos should be abolished because they keep wild animals confined in spaces far smaller than their natural territories, often causing severe psychological distress. Elephants pace endlessly, polar bears wander the edges of their pools, and big cats develop repetitive, harmful behaviours that scientists call stereotypy. For most species, a zoo offers no path back to the wild, so captivity becomes a permanent, shortened sentence. While zoos claim to support conservation, the animals they breed rarely get to live as their own kind, and the funds could be directed toward protecting habitats in the wild, where animals can roam freely. True compassion means recognising that a cage, however well fed, is no home for a creature built for the open world.

A wedding loan can be smart if it's small, short and easy to repay, and dumb if it's large, long and stretched to fund things you'll regret.

The main risk is that you start your marriage already in debt, paying interest on a party that lasts one night. That's especially true for long repayment terms, which can add thousands of dollars to the cost. So before deciding, look at what the loan would actually cover.

**When it can make sense:**
- You want a venue or a photographer you simply can't afford right now, and paying for it over time is clearly cheaper than waiting years.
- You're young and your income is likely to grow quickly, so the payments will feel light in a year or two.
- You'd be locked into a long term at a high rate just to get a deposit or a booking. A shorter loan at a lower rate may be better.

**When to think again:**
- You'd need the loan to cover more than about a third of the total cost.
- The monthly payment would be tight against your other expenses.
- You'd be borrowing against your future savings, like a home down payment.

**Before you sign:**
1. Ask the lender about your actual rate. Rates vary a lot by credit score, so check what you'd qualify for before committing.
2. Look at credit union personal loans specifically. As a member of Harbor Credit Union, you may get better terms than with a big bank.
3. Compare the total cost over the full term, not just the monthly payment.
4. Consider a smaller, cheaper venue, a weekday date, or asking guests to contribute instead of giving gifts.

This is a different case from the English level. "Project lead" describes a role, and in many teams the person who runs the meetings is called the lead, even if they aren't the one hired for it. If your title on paper was "team member", but you regularly led the meetings, made decisions and coordinated the work, then "project lead" is a reasonable way to describe what you did. Recruiters read job titles, and titles vary a lot between companies. What matters more is whether you can show the work.

The line I'd draw is this: don't claim responsibilities you didn't have. If you were never in charge of the budget, the timeline or the people, don't write that you were. In the interview, describe the role in your own words. "I was a member of the team and led the weekly meetings" is a true sentence, and it shows the same skills.

One more thing. If you call yourself lead and the next person doing your reference check was your actual manager, they may say something different. A small gap like this usually does no harm, but a big one can cost you a job offer at the last moment. When you're unsure, write what you actually did and let the details speak for themselves.

This is a different case from the English level, and I think you should be careful here.

A title on a CV is a claim about what you were hired to do and what you were responsible for. "Project lead" tells an employer that you owned the project: you planned it, made decisions, managed risks and were answerable for the result. If you were a team member who sometimes ran meetings, that claim is wider than your actual role.

The risk is real. In many companies a background check or a reference call with your former manager will show the real title. If it doesn't come out until you're hired, you could lose a new job within weeks, over something that was never about your skills. You'd also be starting a new job with a reputation for stretching the truth, which is harder to repair than a slightly smaller title.

But there's an honest way to say it that still works in your favour. Your CV doesn't have to list only your official job title. You can describe what you actually did:

- **Team Member, Project Alpha**
  - Led weekly status meetings and coordinated progress across three teams.
  - Helped plan the project timeline and tracked deliverables.
  - Reported on team progress to senior management.

- **Or, if you want a headline:** "Project Coordinator (team member with responsibility for meeting coordination and progress tracking)"

This is true, and it shows the leadership you're aiming at.

There's one grey area worth knowing. In some companies, people call themselves by the role they acted in, even informally, and hiring managers understand that. That's why it matters less in a casual conversation and more on a CV, where people expect precise claims.

**The Keeper of Black Rock**

On the night of 14 November 1923, the keeper of Black Rock Light, Elias Thorne, found the bottle in his net.

It was not a good night to be hauling nets. The Atlantic had been throwing itself at the island for two days, and the glass of the lantern room had begun to rattle in its frame. Elias had gone out to the lower platform in a oilskin coat and a wool cap, and he came up with a tangle of kelp and three haddock and one bottle, corked with wax and tied with twine that had held its colour far too well.

He brought it inside and set it on the iron stove, where the heat would not touch it. Then he sat at the small table by the window and read the paper inside.

*To whoever finds this: I am off the coast of Iceland, on a trawler called the Hilda. The engine is gone. The water is in the hold. I have a radio, but I have no signal on the port side. If you can see us, light a fire on the shore. The date is 10 November. I am writing this the night before I die, so do not be alarmed if I do not write again.*
*Signed,
Arvidsson, first mate of the Hilda.*

Elias read it twice. Ten November. It was already the fourteenth. He looked at the clock on the wall, and the clock said 11:40. The lamp was due to be trimmed at midnight, and it had not yet been touched.

He went out to the platform and lit the fire in the iron lamp. The flame caught on the wick, and through the great lens it threw a beam across the water. He watched it sweep the horizon for the Hilda. Nothing came into it.

He thought of the fire Arvidsson had asked for. On a dark night, a light on the shore was the thing a ship looked for. His light was the one that told her where the rocks were. He was not sure he could tell the difference to a woman or a man on a boat with the engine dead.

He went back inside and wrote on the back of the paper with a pencil.

*No fire. My light is the danger, not the help. Call the coastguard at St Mary's. They have a radio. Tell them the Hilda is sinking off Iceland, and that I found your note on the fourteenth of November, 1923.*

He did not send it by boat. There was no boat that night, and he knew it. He put the note in the bottle with a fresh sheet of paper, and sealed it in wax.

The next morning, the sea was grey and still, and the gale had gone. Elias took the bottle down to the rowboat and rowed to the mainland, a journey of four hours in the calm. At St Mary's he gave the bottle to the coastguard station and told them about the Hilda.

The man at the station, a Mr Hallett, looked at the paper. "Iceland, you say? That's a long way from here."

"It is," Elias said. "But the note said to call them. Not to send the note."

Hallett looked at him a moment, then picked up the telephone.

Elias did not stay to hear what came of it. He rowed back in the afternoon and lit the lamp at dusk, as he had done every night since 1901.

**Two Weeks Later**

On 28 November, Elias sat at his table mending a net. The lamp had not been trimmed that night, and he had not trimmed it the night before. He had not felt like it.

The bottle came in with the tide. It was caught in the net on the lower platform, and it looked as though the sea had been turning it over and over.

He brought it up and read it.

*From the Coastguard, St Mary's. We have heard from the Hilda. She is not lost. The engine failed on the ninth, not the tenth, and the crew were rescued by a Norwegian vessel on the twelfth. Arvidsson is alive. He is on his way home. He asks that you keep the lamp lit for the winter while he is away. He sends his thanks, and he asks you to keep the light. He is not writing from a deathbed. He wrote that note on the night he thought he would die, and the next day he was on a boat with a working engine. He says the light was not what he saw from the water, but it is what he needs now.*

Elias read the note three times. Then he went up to the lantern room and lit the lamp, though the wick had not needed trimming for three nights.

He sat down on the stone step and wrote in the logbook at the bottom of the page.

*28 November 1923. The Hilda is rescued. Arvidsson, first mate, is alive. The lamp has been lit for the winter. The note is back in my keeping.*

**Three Years Later**

The winter of 1926 was long. On 10 February, the ice came down the channel and shut the mainland in for weeks. The coastguard could not reach the island. The only mail came from the sea, in bottles, or in the nets.

On the evening of 10 February, Elias found another bottle in the net. It was heavier than the first, and the cork was thicker.

He brought it up and read it.

*To Mr Thorne, Black Rock Light. I am Arvidsson. I am back in Iceland. The Hilda was repaired and is sailing again. I have not forgotten the night you rowed to St Mary's with my note, or the night you sat in the dark and did not trim the wick. I am sending you a new lamp, the kind that burns cleaner and needs trimming twice a week instead of once. It will be on the next boat from St Mary's. Please tell me if it arrives. I would also like to know if the light was seen from the ship on that night. I do not know whether it helped, or whether I only think so.*
*Arvidsson*

Elias held the paper against the stove, but he did not let the flame touch it. He went down to the kitchen and wrote back on a fresh sheet.

*Mr Arvidsson. The lamp arrives on the next boat from St Mary's, and I will write to you the moment it does. As for the light: I do not know whether you saw it. I know that on the night you wrote your note, I was the only light on that water, and that is enough for me. Keep the lamp lit for the winter, as you asked. It is my work, and I have done it since 1901.*

He sealed the bottle and set it on the table. Then he went up to the lantern room and lit the lamp, and trimmed the wick, though he had not needed to.

**Six Months Later**

On 10 August, the lamp arrived. It was a new kind, and it burned cleaner than the old one. Elias trimmed it twice a day, as the note had said.

He wrote in the logbook.

*10 August 1924. The lamp has arrived. I trimmed it twice today. I do not know whether Mr Arvidsson ever saw the light from the Hilda. I do not know whether the light saved her. I know that every night since 1901, and tonight, I have lit it, and I will light it again tomorrow.*

He sat down at the table and wrote to Arvidsson.

*Mr Arvidsson. The lamp has arrived. I have trimmed it twice today. I do not know whether you saw the light from the Hilda. I do not know whether the light saved her. I know that every night since 1901, and tonight, I have lit it, and I will light it again tomorrow.*

**One More Entry**

*14 November 1923. The bottle came in with the tide. I have read it three times. I will read it again when the lamp is lit.*

Elias put the paper in the drawer and sat down at the table. The lamp had not been trimmed that night, and he had not trimmed it the night before. He did not know why he had written the date again. He knew why he had written the date. He wrote it down every year on the fourteenth of November, without fail.
